Chain Termination · Dideoxynucleotides · Fragment Separation · Sequence Reading

Knowing the precise order of nucleotides in a DNA molecule was the dream that unlocked the entire genome era. Frederick Sanger's elegant chain-termination method — awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1980 — made that dream a reality and became the gold standard of DNA sequencing for over three decades.
**🎯 Learning Objectives**

items.en: Define DNA sequencing and explain its importance in biology and medicine.
Explain the chain termination principle of the Sanger method.
Describe the role of dNTPs and ddNTPs in Sanger sequencing.
List all components required and describe each step of the Sanger method.
Interpret a sequencing gel and fluorescent chromatogram output.
Discuss the advantages, limitations, and applications of Sanger sequencing.

text.en: **What Is DNA Sequencing?**

DNA sequencing is the process of determining the precise order of the four nucleotide bases — **Adenine (A), Thymine (T), Guanine (G), and Cytosine (C)** — along a strand of DNA. The resulting sequence is the "primary structure" of that DNA molecule.
**Importance in Molecular Biology, Biotechnology, and Genetic Analysis**

items.en: **Gene identification:** Reveals the coding sequences, regulatory regions, and boundaries of genes.
**Mutation detection:** Identifies single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and disease-causing mutations.
**Cloning verification:** Confirms that the correct gene was cloned into the vector and no errors were introduced by PCR.
**Genome projects:** The entire Human Genome Project (3.2 Gb) was sequenced using Sanger sequencing.
**Evolutionary studies:** Comparing sequences across species reveals phylogenetic relationships.
**Forensics and diagnostics:** Pathogen identification, cancer mutation profiling.

text.en: **Introduction to the Sanger Method**

The Sanger method (also called the **chain-termination method or dideoxy method**) was developed by **Frederick Sanger** and colleagues at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge, in 1977. It exploits the ability of DNA polymerase to synthesise a complementary copy of a template strand — but uses specially modified nucleotides that terminate synthesis at known positions, producing a series of DNA fragments whose sizes reveal the sequence.

**Nobel Prize:** Frederick Sanger was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in **1980** for developing this method — his second Nobel Prize (he had won his first in 1958 for protein sequencing). Sanger is one of only four people to have received two Nobel Prizes.
**Chain Termination Principle**

The Sanger method is based on the chain termination (or dideoxy termination) principle: when a **dideoxynucleotide triphosphate (ddNTP)** is incorporated into a growing DNA chain by DNA polymerase, synthesis **stops immediately** — the chain is "terminated." This produces a population of DNA fragments of all possible lengths, each ending at a specific nucleotide type.
**Role of DNA Polymerase**

**DNA polymerase** (modified DNA Pol I — Klenow fragment, or thermostable Taq/T7 polymerase) reads the template strand in the **3'→5' direction** and synthesises a new complementary strand in the **5'→3' direction** by adding dNTPs to the 3'-OH of the growing chain. It requires a primer to initiate synthesis.
**Role of Normal Deoxynucleotides (dNTPs)**
The four standard deoxynucleotide triphosphates — **dATP, dTTP, dGTP, dCTP** — are incorporated normally into the growing chain. Each dNTP provides:

items.en: The **nucleobase** for specific base pairing with the template.
The **deoxyribose sugar** with a free **3'-OH group** that allows the next nucleotide to be added.
**Three phosphate groups** — the outer two are cleaved to release energy for bond formation.

text.en: **Role of Dideoxynucleotides (ddNTPs)**

The four **dideoxynucleotide triphosphates** — **ddATP, ddTTP, ddGTP, ddCTP** — are chemically modified analogues of normal dNTPs. They are identical to dNTPs _except_ that the **3'-OH group on the deoxyribose sugar is replaced by a hydrogen atom (3'-H)**.
**Why Chain Elongation Stops When ddNTP Is Added**
DNA synthesis requires a free **3'-OH group** on the last nucleotide to form a new **3'–5' phosphodiester bond** with the incoming nucleotide. When a ddNTP is incorporated:

items.en: It is paired with the complementary template base (e.g., ddATP pairs with T on template).
The ddNTP is added to the 3' end of the growing chain via its 5'-phosphate.
However, the ddNTP has **no 3'-OH group** (only a 3'-H).
Without a 3'-OH, DNA polymerase **cannot form the next phosphodiester bond**.
Result: DNA synthesis **terminates permanently** at that position.

text.en: **Key Equation:** dNTP (3'-OH) → chain continues | ddNTP (3'-H, no OH) → chain TERMINATES immediately.

**1. Template DNA**
The single-stranded or denatured double-stranded DNA whose sequence is to be determined. Must be pure and in sufficient quantity. Can be a plasmid, PCR product, or genomic fragment.

**2. Primer**
A short synthetic oligonucleotide (18–25 nt) complementary to the template. Provides the free 3'-OH needed for DNA polymerase to start synthesis. Defines the starting point and orientation of sequencing.

**3. DNA Polymerase**
Synthesises the new complementary strand. Requires high fidelity and processivity. Klenow fragment (original), T7 DNA polymerase, or Taq polymerase (cycle sequencing). Lacks 5'→3' exonuclease activity (Klenow/T7).

**4. dNTPs (all four)**
dATP, dTTP, dGTP, dCTP — the normal building blocks for DNA synthesis. Incorporated throughout the growing chain, providing 3'-OH for chain elongation.

**5. ddNTPs (chain terminators)**
ddATP, ddTTP, ddGTP, ddCTP — added at low concentration relative to dNTPs. Each terminates the chain when incorporated. In modern fluorescent Sanger, each ddNTP carries a different fluorescent dye.

**6. Buffer & Conditions**
Appropriate buffer (Tris-HCl, pH 7.5–8.0), MgCl₂ (cofactor for polymerase), denaturing agent (formamide for gel), reaction temperature (37°C for Klenow; 96°C denaturation for cycle sequencing).

**Key Ratio:** ddNTPs are added at a concentration approximately **100× lower** than dNTPs. This ensures that ddNTPs are incorporated randomly and infrequently — producing fragments of all possible lengths, not just very short ones.
Denaturation of Template DNA

The double-stranded template DNA is denatured into single strands by heating (95–96°C) or by treatment with alkali (NaOH). Single-stranded template is essential because DNA polymerase can only copy a single-stranded template.
Primer Annealing

A specific oligonucleotide primer (18–25 nt) is annealed to the template at a complementary sequence upstream of the region to be sequenced. The temperature is lowered (50–60°C) to allow hydrogen bonding between the primer and template.
DNA Synthesis by DNA Polymerase

DNA polymerase extends the primer by adding nucleotides complementary to the template in the 5'→3' direction. All four dNTPs and a small amount of all four ddNTPs are present simultaneously in a single reaction tube (modern fluorescent Sanger method). In the original radioactive method, four separate reactions were used, each containing one type of ddNTP.
Random Incorporation of ddNTPs (Chain Termination)

At each position in the growing chain, the polymerase may incorporate either the normal dNTP (chain continues) or the ddNTP analogue (chain terminates). Because ddNTPs lack a 3'-OH group, synthesis stops permanently at that nucleotide. The random but statistical nature of incorporation means that termination occurs at every possible position in the sequence.
Formation of DNA Fragments of Different Lengths

The sequencing reaction generates a **ladder of DNA fragments** — a population of molecules that all start at the primer and end at every possible position in the template (wherever a ddNTP was incorporated). Each fragment has a defined length and ends with a specific ddNTP:

items.en: Fragments ending in ddATP → terminated at every A position in the new strand.
Fragments ending in ddTTP → terminated at every T position.
Fragments ending in ddGTP → terminated at every G position.
Fragments ending in ddCTP → terminated at every C position.

text.en: Separation by Gel or Capillary Electrophoresis
The mixture of fragments is separated by size using:

items.en: **Denaturing polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE):** Original method. Formamide denatures secondary structures. Fragments migrate through the gel matrix — smaller fragments move faster and migrate farther from the wells. Typically resolves fragments from ~10 to ~1000 nt with single-nucleotide resolution.

**Capillary electrophoresis (CE):** Modern automated method. DNA fragments migrate through a thin capillary tube filled with polymer. Fragments pass a laser detector — each ddNTP carries a different fluorescent dye and emits a different colour when excited.

text.en: Reading of DNA Sequence

**Gel method:** The pattern of bands on the gel is read from bottom (smallest = shortest = closest to the primer end) to top (largest = furthest from primer). The lane containing each band reveals the terminal base at that position.

**Fluorescent capillary method (modern):** The laser detector records fluorescence colour in real time as fragments pass. The output is a **chromatogram (electropherogram)** — coloured peaks, each colour corresponding to one base. The sequence is read from left (small fragments, earliest detected) to right (larger fragments, later detected).
**Reading Fragment Sizes from a Gel**

In the original radioactive Sanger method, four reactions (A, T, G, C) are run in parallel lanes on a denaturing gel. Radioactively labelled fragments appear as dark bands. The sequence is read from the **bottom of the gel upwards** — the lowest band (smallest fragment, i.e., the one nearest the primer) is read first.

At each band position, you record the lane (A, T, G, or C) in which the band appears. Reading upward from position 1 to the top gives the sequence of the new (complementary) strand in the 5'→3' direction.
**Modern Fluorescent Chromatogram (Electropherogram)**
In automated fluorescent Sanger sequencing (Applied Biosystems ABI 3730xl system):

items.en: A single reaction contains all four ddNTPs, each labelled with a **different fluorescent dye**: typically ddA = green, ddT = red, ddG = blue, ddC = purple/black.
Fragments separated by capillary electrophoresis pass a laser — each emits its specific colour.
The detector records a **chromatogram: coloured peaks on a time axis**.
Each peak represents one nucleotide position in the sequence.
The sequence is read from left (smallest fragments = earliest positions) to right.
Base-calling software (e.g., Phred) automatically reads the sequence and assigns quality scores.

text.en: **Read length:** A single Sanger run typically provides **600–1000 reliable base calls** per reaction, with accuracy greater than 99.99% for high-quality regions.
**Sequence Determination from the Template**
The sequence obtained is that of the **newly synthesised strand** (complementary to the template), read in the 5'→3' direction. To obtain the template strand sequence, take the reverse complement.

title.en: Sanger Sequencing Workflow — Click Each Step

text.en: Click any step to expand details.

items.en: 1 🧬 Template DNA Purified single-stranded or double-stranded DNA containing the region to be sequenced. Denatured to single strands by heating at 95°C or treatment with NaOH.
2 🔑 Primer Annealing A specific oligonucleotide primer anneals to the complementary sequence on the template at 50–60°C. Defines the start point and direction of synthesis.

3 ⚗️ DNA Synthesis + ddNTP Termination DNA polymerase extends the primer. All four dNTPs and four fluorescently labelled ddNTPs are present. Randomly, a ddNTP is incorporated at each position, terminating the chain. This produces fragments of every possible length.

4 🔬 Capillary Electrophoresis Denatured fragments loaded into capillary filled with polymer. High-voltage applied — fragments migrate by size (small = fast). Laser detects fluorescent colour as each fragment passes the detection window.

5 📈 Chromatogram Generation Detector records fluorescence intensity over time. Each peak = one base, each colour = one base identity (A=green, T=red, G=blue, C=purple typically). Base-calling software reads the sequence.

6 💻 Sequence Output & Analysis The software outputs the nucleotide sequence as text (e.g., 5'-ATGCATCGA...-3'). Quality scores (Phred) assigned to each base. Sequence aligned against reference databases (BLAST, GenBank) for identification.

text.en: **✅ Advantages**

items.en: **High accuracy:** Error rate <0.001%; considered the "gold standard" for accuracy.
**Long read length:** 600–1000 reliable bases per run.
**Well-established:** Decades of optimisation; robust and reproducible.
**Cost-effective for small targets:** Ideal for sequencing single genes, verifying clones, detecting point mutations.
**Widely used:** Standard method in clinical diagnostics, forensics, and research labs.
**Automated:** ABI 3730xl can run 384 samples simultaneously.

text.en: **⚠️ Limitations**

items.en: **Limited throughput:** Maximum ~1 kb per reaction; sequencing an entire genome requires millions of reactions.
**Expensive for whole genomes:** The Human Genome Project (Sanger-based) cost ~$3 billion.
**Cannot sequence GC-rich or repetitive regions easily:** Secondary structures cause compression artefacts.
**First ~15–40 bases unreliable** (primer region — poor resolution at very short lengths).
**Requires pure, single template:** Mixtures of sequences give ambiguous chromatograms.

text.en: **Brief Comparison with Modern Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS)**

Next-generation sequencing (NGS) technologies (Illumina, PacBio, Oxford Nanopore) can sequence billions of base pairs simultaneously at very low cost (~$0.001/Mb vs ~$0.50/Mb for Sanger). However, Sanger remains the preferred method for validating single-gene mutations, confirming cloning results, and clinical diagnostic applications requiring high accuracy and long reads.

**Gene Analysis**
Determining the complete nucleotide sequence of a gene, its intron-exon organisation, promoter, and regulatory elements.

**Mutation Detection**
Identifying single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), point mutations, insertions, and deletions associated with genetic diseases (e.g., cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease, BRCA1/2 in cancer).

**Confirmation of Cloned DNA**
Verifying that a gene was correctly inserted into a vector during cloning and that no PCR errors or mutations were introduced.

**Human Genome Project**
Sanger sequencing was the primary technology used to sequence the entire 3.2 Gb human genome (1990–2003), leading to the identification of ~20,000–25,000 human genes.

**Medical Diagnostics**
Clinical sequencing of pathogen genomes (HIV drug resistance monitoring, SARS-CoV-2 variant identification), BRCA1/2 testing, pharmacogenomics.

**Forensic Science**
DNA fingerprinting and identification using mitochondrial DNA sequencing for forensic investigations and species identification.

text.en: **⚗️ Chain Termination Principle — Exam Key Points**
Core Principle

items.en: ddNTPs lack a **3'-OH group** (they have 3'-H instead).
DNA polymerase requires a 3'-OH to catalyse the next phosphodiester bond.
When ddNTP is incorporated → chain terminates permanently at that position.
dNTPs are added at ~100× higher concentration than ddNTPs — ensures all possible fragment lengths are produced.
The sequence is determined by which ddNTP terminated each fragment and the fragment's length.

text.en: **Exam tip:** The ONLY structural difference between dNTP and ddNTP is the 3' position: dNTP has 3'-OH, ddNTP has 3'-H. This single difference is the entire basis of Sanger sequencing.
**🔬 Original vs Modern Sanger Sequencing**
Methodology
**📈 Reading a Sequencing Gel — Exam Guidance**
Gel Interpretation

items.en: The gel has four lanes: ddA, ddT, ddG, ddC (each lane contains fragments terminated by that ddNTP).
Smallest fragments (fewest nucleotides from primer) are at the **bottom** (run furthest in gel).
Read the sequence from **bottom to top** — the lowest band is position 1.
At each band position, record which lane (A, T, G, or C) contains the band.
The sequence obtained is the **new (complementary) strand** read 5'→3'.
Example: if from bottom to top you have bands in lanes A, T, G, C, A → sequence is 5'-ATGCA-3'.

text.en: **Exam tip:** Always read gel bottom-to-top (small fragments = closer to primer = read first in 5'→3' direction). Modern chromatograms are read left-to-right (same logic — smaller fragments elute first).
**🏥 Applications — Exam Key Points**
Applications

items.en: Developed by **Frederick Sanger (1977)** — Nobel Prize Chemistry 1980.
Used to sequence the **Human Genome Project (1990–2003)**.
Gold standard for **mutation detection** in clinical settings (BRCA1/2, CFTR, etc.).
Routine use: **verification of recombinant DNA constructs** after cloning.
Accurate read length: **600–1000 bp** per reaction, >99.99% accuracy.
Phred quality scores assigned to each base by base-calling software.

text.en: **Click-to-Reveal Key Definitions**

answer.en: Dideoxynucleoside triphosphate. A synthetic analogue of a normal dNTP with H at the 3' position instead of OH. When incorporated by DNA polymerase, it permanently terminates chain elongation because the next phosphodiester bond cannot be formed without a 3'-OH group.

The permanent halting of DNA synthesis when a ddNTP is incorporated into the growing chain. Because ddNTPs lack a 3'-OH group, DNA polymerase cannot add the next nucleotide — the chain is irreversibly terminated at that position.

The single-stranded or denatured DNA molecule whose nucleotide sequence is to be determined. DNA polymerase reads the template in the 3'→5' direction to synthesise the new complementary strand in the 5'→3' direction.

A short (18–25 nt) synthetic oligonucleotide complementary to the template strand, upstream of the region to be sequenced. Provides the free 3'-OH group needed for DNA polymerase to initiate synthesis and defines the start position of the sequence read.

A technique that separates charged molecules by size in an electric field. In Sanger sequencing, denatured DNA fragments migrate through a gel or capillary — smaller fragments travel faster and farther, allowing fragments differing by a single nucleotide to be resolved.

The graphical output (electropherogram) of automated fluorescent Sanger sequencing. Coloured peaks on a time axis represent individual nucleotides detected as fluorescently labelled fragments pass the laser detector in the capillary electrophoresis instrument.

A quality score assigned to each base call in automated Sanger sequencing. Q = -10 × log₁₀(P), where P is the error probability. Phred Q20 = 99% accuracy; Q30 = 99.9% accuracy. High-quality Sanger sequence typically has Phred scores >40.

A modern, automated alternative to slab gel electrophoresis used in Sanger sequencing. DNA fragments migrate through a thin (~75 µm) capillary filled with polymer. A laser detects fluorescence as each fragment passes — provides higher resolution, speed, and throughput than traditional gel electrophoresis.

text.en: **Sanger Method**Developed by Frederick Sanger in 1977 (Nobel Prize 1980). Also called chain-termination or dideoxy method. The gold standard for DNA sequencing.
**Key Principle**Uses ddNTPs as chain terminators. ddNTPs lack a 3'-OH group → when incorporated, chain synthesis stops permanently.
**dNTP vs ddNTP**Only structural difference: dNTP has 3'-OH; ddNTP has 3'-H (no OH). This single difference prevents the next phosphodiester bond formation.
**Fragment Ladder**Reaction produces fragments of all possible lengths, each ending at a specific nucleotide type. Reading fragment sizes in order reveals the sequence.
**dNTP:ddNTP Ratio**ddNTPs are ~100× more dilute than dNTPs to ensure random incorporation at every position — producing the complete ladder of fragment sizes.
**Original Method**Four separate reactions (ddA, ddT, ddG, ddC), radioactive labelling, 4-lane polyacrylamide gel, read bottom to top, autoradiography.
**Modern Method**Single reaction, four fluorescently labelled ddNTPs (each different colour), capillary electrophoresis, chromatogram output, automated base calling.
**Gel Reading**Read bottom to top (smallest = earliest position). Each band's lane/colour = the nucleotide at that position. Sequence is the new strand read 5'→3'.
**Read Length & Accuracy**600–1000 reliable bases per run; >99.99% accuracy for high-quality bases. First 15–40 bases may be unreliable.
**Applications**Clone verification, mutation detection, Human Genome Project, clinical diagnostics, pathogen identification, forensics.

**Limitation vs NGS**Only ~1 kb per reaction (low throughput); expensive for whole genomes. NGS sequences billions of bases simultaneously but Sanger remains gold standard for accuracy in targeted sequencing.
**Correct Step Order**Denature DNA → Anneal primer → Polymerase extends + ddNTP terminates → Fragments of all sizes form → Electrophoresis separates → Read sequence from chromatogram.

definition.en: The process of determining the precise order of nucleotide bases (A, T, G, C) along a DNA strand. The sequence reveals the genetic information encoded in the DNA molecule.

A DNA sequencing technique developed by Frederick Sanger in 1977, based on the chain-termination principle using dideoxynucleotides. Also called the dideoxy method. Gold standard of DNA sequencing for over 30 years.

A synthetic analogue of a normal deoxyribonucleotide triphosphate (dNTP), lacking a 3'-OH group (replaced by 3'-H). When incorporated by DNA polymerase, it permanently terminates chain elongation. Used as chain terminators in Sanger sequencing.
The permanent halting of DNA synthesis caused by incorporation of a ddNTP. Since ddNTPs lack a 3'-OH group, no new phosphodiester bond can be formed — the growing chain cannot be extended further.

The single-stranded DNA molecule used as the blueprint in DNA synthesis. In Sanger sequencing, the template strand is read 3'→5' by DNA polymerase, which synthesises a new complementary strand in the 5'→3' direction.

A short (18–25 nt) synthetic single-stranded oligonucleotide complementary to the template strand. Provides the free 3'-OH required for DNA polymerase to initiate synthesis. Defines the start and direction of sequencing in Sanger method.

A technique that uses an electric field to separate charged molecules (such as DNA fragments) by size. Smaller fragments migrate faster and farther in the gel or capillary. Enables single-nucleotide resolution of Sanger sequencing fragments.

The graphical output of automated fluorescent Sanger sequencing showing coloured peaks on a time axis. Each peak represents one nucleotide — the peak colour identifies the base (A/T/G/C) and peak position reflects fragment size.

A modern, automated separation method used in Sanger sequencing where DNA fragments migrate through a thin polymer-filled capillary tube. Laser detection of fluorescence allows high-resolution, high-throughput sequencing (e.g., ABI 3730xl platform).
Deoxynucleoside triphosphate — the normal building block of DNA. Contains a deoxyribose sugar with a free 3'-OH group that allows continued chain elongation. Four types: dATP, dTTP, dGTP, dCTP.

text.en: Click each question to expand answer hints.
**1. What is the principle of Sanger's chain termination method of DNA sequencing?**
**Answer Hints:**

items.en: Principle: chain-termination (dideoxy method) using dideoxynucleotide triphosphates (ddNTPs) as chain terminators.
ddNTPs are structural analogues of normal dNTPs but lack a 3'-OH group (have 3'-H instead).
DNA polymerase incorporates ddNTPs into the growing chain at random positions — when ddNTP is incorporated, no further elongation is possible (no 3'-OH for next phosphodiester bond).
This produces a population of fragments of all possible lengths, each starting at the primer and ending at a specific base type.
Separation by electrophoresis and reading the positions gives the complete sequence.
Developed by Frederick Sanger in 1977 (Nobel Prize Chemistry 1980).

text.en: **2. Why does the incorporation of a dideoxynucleotide (ddNTP) cause chain termination? Explain with reference to its structure.**
**Answer Hints:**

items.en: Normal dNTP has: 5'-triphosphate, deoxyribose sugar with 2'-H and 3'-OH, and a nucleobase.
ddNTP differs in ONE critical way: the 3' position of the deoxyribose sugar has a hydrogen atom (3'-H) instead of a hydroxyl group (3'-OH).
DNA polymerase extends a chain by catalysing an attack of the 3'-OH on the α-phosphate of the incoming dNTP, forming a new 3'–5' phosphodiester bond and releasing pyrophosphate.

When a ddNTP is incorporated: its 5'-phosphate forms a bond with the previous nucleotide's 3'-OH. But the ddNTP itself now sits at the 3' end with only a 3'-H — no hydroxyl group is available to attack the next incoming nucleotide.
Therefore, no new phosphodiester bond can form → synthesis is permanently halted → chain termination.
Include a structural diagram comparing dNTP and ddNTP showing the 3'-OH vs 3'-H difference.

text.en: **3. Describe the steps involved in Sanger DNA sequencing. How is the sequence determined from the result?**
**Answer Hints:**

items.en: Step 1: Denature template DNA to single strands (heat or NaOH).
Step 2: Anneal oligonucleotide primer to template (50–60°C).
Step 3: Add DNA polymerase, all four dNTPs, and all four fluorescently labelled ddNTPs (100× lower concentration than dNTPs).
Step 4: Synthesis proceeds; at each position, ddNTP may be randomly incorporated → chain terminates at every possible position → population of fragments of all lengths is produced.
Step 5: Fragments denatured and loaded into capillary electrophoresis instrument.
Step 6: Fragments separated by size; laser detects fluorescent colour as each fragment elutes.
Sequence determination: chromatogram shows coloured peaks; each colour = one base; peaks read left to right (small = earliest in 5'→3' sequence).

text.en: **4. What is the role of dNTPs and ddNTPs in Sanger sequencing? Why are ddNTPs added at a much lower concentration than dNTPs?**
**Answer Hints:**

items.en: **Role of dNTPs:** Normal building blocks — provide the nucleotide subunits for DNA chain elongation. All four (dATP, dTTP, dGTP, dCTP) are needed. Their 3'-OH groups allow the chain to continue growing.

**Role of ddNTPs:** Chain terminators — incorporated randomly at complementary positions and permanently stop synthesis. Each one terminates at a specific base type. In modern sequencing, each carries a different fluorescent dye for base identification.

**Why low concentration of ddNTPs?** If ddNTPs were in equal or higher concentration, almost every fragment would be very short (terminated near the primer). A low ddNTP:dNTP ratio (~1:100) ensures that termination occurs rarely and randomly across the entire length of the template — generating fragments of every possible length from position 1 to ~1000 nt. This complete "ladder" of fragment sizes is essential for reading the full sequence.

text.en: **5. List the components required for Sanger sequencing. State the advantages and limitations of this method.**
**Answer Hints:**

items.en: **Components:** (1) Template DNA (single-stranded); (2) Primer (specific oligonucleotide); (3) DNA polymerase (Klenow fragment, T7, or Taq); (4) All four dNTPs (dATP, dTTP, dGTP, dCTP); (5) All four ddNTPs (ddATP, ddTTP, ddGTP, ddCTP — each fluorescently labelled); (6) Buffer with Mg²⁺ cofactor.
**Advantages:** High accuracy (>99.99%); long reads (600–1000 bp); gold standard; automated; cost-effective for single genes.
**Limitations:** Low throughput (only ~1 kb per reaction); expensive for whole genomes; first 15–40 bases unreliable; cannot sequence repetitive regions well; requires pure single-sequence template.
Brief mention of NGS as higher-throughput alternative, but Sanger remains preferred for targeted, high-accuracy sequencing.
